hero.h1: Service accounts, API keys and AI agents under control.
hero.lead: Every employee has a joiner and a leaver process. The many technical accounts, secrets and agents working in your systems usually have neither. We bring them into your identity governance, with an inventory, an accountable owner, a lifecycle and tightly scoped access.

sections.heading: Why standard IGA processes miss these accounts
paragraphs: Identity governance is built for people. An account starts with an employment contract, a manager confirms the access, and it is disabled when the person leaves. A service account has no contract, an API key has no manager, and a certificate expires without anyone being asked.

Auditors know the result: service accounts with domain admin rights whose purpose nobody remembers, secrets in source code that have been valid for years, and accounts from finished projects that still work.
NIS2 and DORA make no distinction between people and machines when it comes to access control. Technical accounts face the same requirements for inventory, access granting and evidence.

items.title: Inventory
items.text: We find service accounts, secrets, certificates, workload identities and AI agents across Active Directory, Entra ID, cloud platforms and SaaS applications.

items.title: Ownership
items.text: Every technical identity gets an accountable owner who knows its purpose and confirms its access.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text: Creation, recertification and retirement run through defined processes in your IGA platform.

items.title: Short-lived credentials
items.text: Where possible, we replace standing secrets with managed identities, workload identity federation and vaults with rotation.

items.title: Least privilege and monitoring
items.text: We cut access down to what is needed, log its use and make deviations visible.

items.title: Governance for AI agents
items.text: For every agent we define identity, delegation, scope of access and logging, for example with Microsoft Entra Agent ID.

sections.heading: AI agents: what is different
paragraphs: An AI agent reads email, books meetings, changes records or calls other systems, often on behalf of a user. For every action, that raises two questions: whose rights apply right now, and who approved them?

We treat agents as identities in their own right, each with an accountable owner. They get only the access their task needs, delegated rights are limited in time and scope, critical actions need human approval, and every action can be traced to both the agent and the user who triggered it.

sections.heading: How we work
sections.intro: Four steps. After each one, you decide whether and how to continue.

items.title: Inventory and risk analysis
items.text: We record the technical identities in your most important systems and rate them by access, age, usage and ownership.

items.title: Target model and rules
items.text: We define how technical identities are created, who owns them, how often they are reviewed and when they end, and which platform handles what.

items.title: Implementation
items.text: We clean up, assign owners, introduce rotation and short-lived credentials, and connect the processes to your IGA or PAM platform.

items.title: Operations
items.text: Recertifications, reports and alerts become part of daily operations. If you want, we run them for you.

items.a: Any identity that does not belong to a person: service accounts, technical users, API keys, certificates, workload identities, bots and AI agents.

items.q: Do we need a dedicated NHI tool?
items.a: Not necessarily. Many requirements can be covered with your existing IGA, PAM or cloud platform. We assess this vendor-neutrally and recommend an additional tool only when it closes a specific gap.

items.q: How do you find service accounts nobody has documented?
items.a: We analyse directories, sign-in logs, cloud configurations and vaults, then check the results with system owners. Accounts nobody claims are disabled in a controlled way and monitored before they are deleted.

items.q: How does this relate to NIS2 and DORA?
items.a: Both require provable control over access, whether a person or a machine is accessing. Technical accounts without an accountable owner are a common audit finding.
